fields.Q1:
WHAT IS STANDING AROUND THIS ROOM MADE OF?**

Cut stone blocks laid in courses — dry, square, mortared masonry. That is what magnification says. **At the size the image is presented, I cannot tell, because I cannot see it.** If you asked me from the 1:1 view what I'd put a hand on, my honest answer is "nothing — there's a lit floor and then it stops."
fields.Q1_WHY: The material call comes entirely from a gamma lift (I raised the image ~3.3× to read it). Under that lift, the band at x0–55, y235–775 and the band at x55–645, y198–230 resolve into large rectangular blocks with regular horizontal mortar courses roughly every 55–60px and a vertical seam near x≈40. Unlifted, those same regions measure: north band mean L **9–17**, peak 32; left band mean **10.4**, peak 20; south slab mean **11.5**. The floor 60px from the lamp measures mean **122**, peak **231**. The standing structure sits at **4–7% of the floor's luminance**. There is no display that renders 10/255 as stone.
fields.Q2:
SOLID MASS, OR FLAT PATTERN AROUND THE EDGE?**

**Flat pattern.** Not because it's drawn thin — the north band genuinely has thickness in plan, ~32px from y198 to the mortar line at y230 — but because nothing in the rendering carries mass:

- No cast shadow anywhere. The block at (183,452)–(248,522) is the only piece of structure inside the lit radius. The lamp is 220px east of it. West of it, (160–182, 460–515) measures **21.1**; the floor at the same 225px radius on other bearings measures 24–42. That's falloff, not occlusion. A solid object of any height throws nothing here.
- No side face, no cap/edge value split, no ambient-occlusion darkening at the base of anything.
- Light passes through the north band unattenuated. Column x=340 (inside wall mass) and column x=405 (inside the open passage) climb in lockstep as they approach the lamp: 10.3→20.8→33.8→48.7 vs 6.5→15.6→44.7→57.3. The wall is being lit exactly as if it were floor.

The block at (183,452) is the clearest case: it's a rectangle with a 3px dark outline on all four sides and nothing else. It is a sticker on the floor.
fields.Q3:
WHERE EXACTLY DOES THE GROUND STOP?**

Three different answers on three sides, which is itself the finding.

**North** — a real, hard edge. Vertical scan at x=150: y190–197 = (1,1,2), dead flat. y198 jumps to (9,9,12) and holds to y229. y230–233 drops to (2,2,2) — a 4px mortar line. y234 onward is floor at 3–9. So the transition is **1px** into the band and **4px** out of it. Total contrast across the whole event: 1 → 11 → 2 → 6. Eleven units.

**East and south** — the ground does not stop. x646–750 measures mean 8.8, max 29, and magnified it is unmistakably the *same floor asset* as the interior: irregular blocks with diagonal hatch scratches. The apparent edge at x≈645 is the light falloff and nothing else. Same at the bottom.

**West** — a genuine asset change at x=55: hard vertical seam, large smooth courses to the left, hatched irregular floor blocks to the right. Real boundary, ~1px transition, ~4 units of luminance across it.
fields.Q4:
WHAT IS HOLDING THIS PLACE TOGETHER?**

**Effectively NOTHING.** No rope, no driven pins, no hide, no timber, no bracing, no shoring, no patch, no strap, no wedge. Nothing anywhere on the standing structure is doing structural work or shows anyone ever intervened.

The only candidates are three marks, all found by magnification: a vertical post with three horizontal crossbars at **(133–147, 190–227)**; a plain vertical post at **(565–570, 190–228)**; and a third rung-triplet at **(541–557, 700–775)**. Each is ~14px wide, sits 1–3 luminance units above its surround, and holds nothing — they read as ladder rungs or markers, not as fixings. Cut all three and nothing moves.

For a place defined as four hundred years of continuous emergency repair, this is the largest gap in the image.
fields.Q5:
BUILT, OR AN IMAGE THAT WAS REPEATED?**

**Built.** I tested for this rather than assuming. Exact 28×28 block matching across the north band found 18 duplicate pairs and no group larger than 2 — negligible. Vertical autocorrelation on the left band and horizontal on the north band show a smooth monotonic curve with no periodic minimum: no lock-in at 16, 32, 48 or any tile pitch. Block widths and course heights vary irregularly. Nothing is stamped.

Credit where due: the layout is authored, not tiled. The problem is not repetition.
fields.Q6:
WOULD YOU BELIEVE THIS SHIPPED?**

**YES.** At 1:1 it reads as a warm lamplit floor with a character on it, which is a perfectly plausible shipped roguelike frame.

Merely competent, or genuinely good? **The standing structure is below competent.** Not "fine," not "promising" — it fails the only job a wall has in a top-down game, which is to tell you where you can't go. The floor is doing all the work in this image and it is doing it well; the walls are contributing a value fill and a mortar grid at a brightness nobody will ever see.
fields.Q7:
WHAT CAN YOU ACTUALLY SEE ON THE STANDING SURFACES AT 1:1?**

**Nothing.** Every standing surface is blank at 1:1.

Legible at 1:1: the lit floor; the figure; the block at (183,452)–(248,522) as an undifferentiated pale rectangle; and a faint suggestion of a lighter vertical channel around x380–440 running north. That is the complete list.

Only under magnification: the mortar courses of the left band; the block structure of the north band; the two posts and the rung triplets; the arch-or-niche shape at roughly (0–55, 500–580); the fact that the south slab exists at all.

Does it change with distance from the figure? No — and that's the point. **There is no standing surface anywhere near the lamp.** The figure is at (408,487); the nearest boundary is the north band at 252px and the left band at 353px. The light has fully decayed before it reaches any wall. So the answer is uniform: blank at every distance, on every side.

I want to be exact about one thing: I did not see the walls and then judge them dark. I read the image at 1:1 first and described a lit floor surrounded by darkness. The structure only came into existence for me after I lifted the gamma. That is hunting, not seeing.
fields.Q7_WHY:
Checked at 1:1 — (55–645, 198–235) north band; (0–55, 235–775) left band; (60–640, 775–830) south slab; (183–248, 452–522) the interior block; (310–500, 0–195) north mass. Had to magnify — (110–175, 185–245) post with crossbars; (540–600, 180–240) plain post; (0–60, 480–590) arch/niche; (280–530, 180–300) north gap at 4×; (640–750, 230–780) east region.

There is a second, harder measure here. After normalising brightness entirely — full gamma lift, so darkness is no longer a factor — mean local gradient is: floor **5.61**, north band **1.34**, left band **1.68**, south slab **0.82**, void **0.00**. The walls aren't merely unlit. They carry a quarter of the floor's detail even when you correct for the lighting. The south slab at 0.82 is nearer to the empty void than to the floor. It is a featureless grey rectangle 580px wide.
fields.Q8:
ANYTHING YOUR EYE KEEPS RETURNING TO?**

Two things.

The **rung-and-post motif** appears three times — (133–147, 190–227), (565–570, 190–228), (541–557, 700–775) — always as a vertical bar with horizontal crossbars, always at a boundary, always at the same scale. Three instances of the only detail in the image is enough to feel like a motif rather than a placement.

The **isolated bright patch at approximately (455–500, 40–200)** inside the north wall mass. At y=120 it measures 15.4–15.5 against 9.9–10.1 for the masonry either side of it — the brightest thing in that whole region, and it is 400px from the lamp with nothing between. It has no explanation. My eye kept going back to it looking for one.
fields.Q9:
WHAT IS BEYOND THE WALLS?**

Two categorically different things, and the image gives you no way to tell them apart at 1:1.

Above y≈195, outside x310–500, the pixels are exactly **(1,1,2) with zero variance** across the entire region. Not dark — *empty*. Authored void. Nothing was drawn there.

Everywhere else — east of x=645, south of y=775 — is **more of the same place, simply unlit**. It measures 8–12 with real block structure in it, and at magnification the east side is verifiably the same floor asset as the interior.

So: to the north, nothing exists. To the east and south, the dungeon continues and you just can't see it. Both render as black. The player has no way to distinguish "the map ends" from "the lamp ends," which is a navigational problem, not just an aesthetic one.
fields.Q10:
COULD YOU TELL A WAY THROUGH FROM A DEAD END WITHOUT WALKING INTO IT?**

Found it: **x≈377–437, running north from y≈330 to the top of the frame.** About 60px, two tiles wide.

**I read it as a passage — barely, and for the wrong reason.** What tipped me was not the gap; it was that the region above y=195 at x310–500 has *content* while the regions either side of it are flat (1,1,2) void. I inferred a corridor from the shape of the authored area, not from the structure.

The gap itself actively works against you. At y=120, the open passage measures **5.7–9.1** and the flanking wall measures **9.9–10.1**. **The way through is darker than the wall.** The sign is inverted, and the magnitude — one to four units out of 255 — is below any perceptual threshold on any screen. There is no threshold, no jamb, no doorframe, no change of floor material, no light spill down the corridor mouth.

Answer to the question as asked: **no.** Not from the structure. I got there by reading the render's authored/unauthored boundary, which is an artefact, not a design affordance.
fields.Q11:
HAS ANYTHING HAPPENED TO THIS STRUCTURE?**

Nothing has happened to it. It is **intact, square and unmarked**.

Read from: mortar courses in the left band run unbroken from y235 to y775 at a consistent 55–60px pitch with no interruption; every block corner is square; there is no rubble, no spall, no gap, no missing block, no slump, no patch, no shoring, no soot, no water track, no staining. The diagonal hatch-scratches that read as wear belong to the *floor* asset, not to the walls — the left band and the south slab have none at all. The south slab (0.82 local gradient) is as clean as a fresh fill.

Against the brief — four hundred years of continuous heavy use, endless repair, never once cared for — the walls read as newly cut. Whatever history this place has, it happened to the ground and not to the things standing on it.
fields.CULL: > Walls sit at 4–7% of floor luminance — at 1:1 the room has no visible structure, only darkness.
fields.FLIP LIST:
- Raise all standing structure to a hard luminance floor of ~35–45 regardless of distance, so walls read as *dark stone* rather than as absence — the north band, left band and south slab currently sit at 9–17.
- Make the boundary itself legible: a consistent 2–4px inner edge on every wall face at (55,198)–(645,230), (0–55, 235–775) and (60–640, 775+), so the room has an outline that survives at 1:1 without light.
- Give the north passage mouth at x377–437 an inverted read — passage floor brighter than the flanking mass, plus a jamb or threshold — instead of the current 5.7 vs 10.0 that makes the way out darker than the wall.
- Cast shadows from standing mass. The block at (183,452)–(248,522) is 220px from the lamp and throws nothing; a hard west-facing shadow there is the single cheapest thing that would make anything in this image read as solid.
- Put the orcs' work on the walls: rope, driven pins, hide, salvaged timber at the mortar lines and corners — currently the entire standing structure carries three 14px rung-marks and is otherwise unmaintained-looking only in the sense of being untouched, which is the opposite of the brief.
